name: function-composition
intent: Combine a chain of small unary transformations into one reusable function by sequencing them with a composition combinator (compose/pipe), so the order of the steps is stated once, every step stays independently testable, and the chain itself becomes a value that can be named, passed and reassembled.
problem: A transformation that is naturally a sequence of small pure steps gets written as nested calls or as repeated imperative assignment (`h(g(f(x)))`, or `y = f(x); y = g(y); ...; return y`) at every call site. The order is duplicated wherever the chain is used, the intermediate values need throwaway names, steps cannot be reused in a different order, and changing one stage means editing every copy.
context: Pure or nearly pure value transformations - parsing, normalisation, validation, formatting, pricing, AST rewriting - where each step is unary and the language treats functions as values. It pays off when the chain is reused or assembled from data (configuration, plugin lists, per-request policy), when steps must be unit-tested in isolation, and when the same steps must also run element-wise over a collection or lazily over a stream. It stops applying where steps need side effects or branching between stages: there the shell around the pure core owns control flow.
benefits: The chain becomes a value: it can be named, stored, passed to higher-order code (map, retry, configuration) and extended by composing it further, instead of being retyped at each call site.
Each step is small, unary and pure, so it can be tested and reasoned about in isolation; composition preserves those tests because the composed function only sequences them.
Order and membership of the chain can be data: assembling the steps from configuration or a registry changes behaviour without editing the steps themselves.
Intermediate values stop needing names, and a left-to-right pipe/andThen chain reads in execution order, which is easier to review than nested calls that read inside-out.
Associativity means a chain can be regrouped - split for reuse, fused for a hot path, or reordered in tests - without changing its meaning, because composition only sequences function application.

It reuses the language's existing higher-order vocabulary (lambdas, std::function, java.util.function.Function, closures, proc composition, Function1 combinators) instead of introducing an orchestration class.
tradeoffs: One extra call frame per step, and combinators that erase the callable (std::function, Function chains, Box<dyn Fn>) can defeat inlining and allocate on the way into a hot loop.
Anonymous chains destroy diagnostic context: production stack traces and profilers show lambda frames or the combinator's internals instead of the failing step's name.

Point-free composition has nowhere to put branching, short-circuiting or error handling; as soon as a step may fail or skip, the composition must be lifted into a Result/Option/monad layer with its own concepts, or abandoned for explicit control flow.
Steps must all be unary and end-to-end type-compatible; adapting existing multi-argument functions drags partial application or currying into the codebase as a second, unfamiliar concept.
Type inference degrades along the chain: Java wildcard capture, TypeScript overload resolution, Kotlin and Swift inference report errors inside the combinator instead of at the offending step.
Direction conventions differ (right-to-left classic compose vs left-to-right pipe/andThen); a codebase that mixes libraries with different argument order can reverse a chain silently.

participants.responsibility: A small unary transformation - one input, one output, no side effects - that performs a single stage of the chain and can be tested and reused on its own.

Higher-order function (compose, pipe, andThen) that takes two or more steps and returns a new function applying them in a fixed order; it fixes the ordering convention and provides the identity element for the zero-step case.
The new unary function produced by the combinator: the reusable value that names the whole chain and can be stored, passed or applied.
Partial application, currying or a thin wrapper that reduces a multi-argument function to the unary shape the chain needs; kept at the edge so the steps themselves stay composable.
Supplies the input and interprets the result; owns I/O and control flow so the steps can stay pure (functional core, imperative shell).

use_cases: Input normalisation: trim, parse, canonicalise and validate a payload before it reaches domain logic, with the same chain reused by HTTP handlers and message consumers.
Pricing and rule chains: base price, discount, tax and rounding applied in a fixed, configurable order to an immutable value object.
Compiler and AST work: a pass list of rewrite functions composed once and applied over the tree, with passes added or reordered per optimisation level.
Serialisation and formatting: sanitise, format, encode and sign a document, where each step is tested separately and the composed chain is stored as a constant.
Data transformation over collections: the same pure steps composed into one function and passed to map/filter/stream operations, so element-wise processing reuses the chain.
Policy assembly at startup: the processing chain is built from configuration or plugin registrations and then applied per request without further branching.
Reactive stream processing: RxJS Observable.pipe chains the same logical steps across asynchronous event sequences, with operators composed once and reused across streams.

ETL and data pipeline transformation: extract-transform-load chains where each stage (parse, clean, enrich, aggregate, write) is a unary pure function composed into a reusable pipeline run over batches or streaming data.

HTTP request/response middleware: the middleware stack is a composed function chain where each layer (authenticate, authorise, rate-limit, deserialize, validate) is a unary handler; composition is resolved once at startup.

Matrix and vector transformations in numerical code: each linear algebra operation (scale, rotate, translate, project) is a unary function on a matrix type; composing them once builds the transformation pipeline that is applied to every vertex or pixel.
Ramda pipelines: R.pipe and R.compose assemble reusable data-last transformations from small functions, centralising the order while letting the same composed value run over many inputs.
Redux store setup: Redux's compose helper combines store enhancers right-to-left into one enhancer, so the enhancer order is defined once instead of reconstructed at each store boundary.
lodash/fp transformations: lodash/fp's auto-curried, data-last compose/flow helpers assemble immutable-friendly transformations from reusable steps that can be passed as values.
avoid_when: Two or three fixed calls used in one place: nested calls or named intermediate variables are clearer than introducing a combinator.
Steps must mutate shared state or perform I/O between stages: keep an explicit sequence, or confine the effects to a shell around a pure core.
Each stage can branch or fail: use explicit control flow, a Result/Option type with its own andThen, or a pipeline object that names stages and errors, instead of raw function composition.
The chain runs per element in a performance-critical loop: a fused loop written by hand beats a chain of indirect calls.
The whole transformation is a one-off expression: a single well-named function that calls the steps in order documents intent better than a combinator.
anti_patterns: Point-free heroics: dropping argument names until the dataflow can no longer be read - five anonymous lambdas in a row with no step names.
Composing side-effecting steps (logging, mutation, metrics) and calling the result pure; the order of the invisible effects now depends on chain order.
Mixing right-to-left compose and left-to-right pipe/andThen helpers in one codebase, so a copied chain can run in reverse.
Re-inventing the combinator at every call site instead of naming the chain once, which recreates exactly the duplicated order the pattern removes.
Assembling a chain from steps whose types were widened to a common supertype (Object, any, String -> String), losing the compile-time guarantee that each output fits the next input.
design_principles: Single responsibility: each step performs exactly one transformation, at one level of abstraction.
Referential transparency: composition is only meaningful for steps whose output depends solely on their input; effects belong to the shell.
Composition over inheritance: sequence and vary behaviour by composing functions instead of subclassing or templating an orchestration class.
Open/closed: new behaviour arrives as a new step or a new arrangement of steps, without editing existing ones.
Smallest useful interface: a unary function is the narrowest contract a stage can have, which is what makes the pieces interchangeable.
best_practices: Name the chain once as a function or constant and reuse it; do not rebuild the same pipeline at several call sites.
Keep steps small, pure and named; reserve inline lambdas for trivial glue and for adapting arity.
Pick one ordering convention for the codebase (prefer left-to-right pipe/andThen) and apply it everywhere, including in tests.
Give the composed value an explicit type (an interface, a function type, a std::function boundary) so inference stops at the definition instead of inside the combinator.
Keep I/O, logging and metrics in the caller; pass pure steps into the chain.
Test the steps individually and the assembled chain with order-sensitive cases, including the empty and single-step chains (the identity element).
Use type signatures at composition boundaries so the compiler catches a step whose output no longer fits the next step's input — type errors surface at the composition site, not at every call site.
Test the identity element explicitly: verify that id ∘ f = f ∘ id = f holds for each step; a failing identity law signals a step with hidden state or side effects.
Name each step with a descriptive identifier; even when using anonymous lambdas for arity adaptation, wrap them with a named constant so stack traces and profiler output remain readable.

Profile the composed chain in its actual production hot path: each step adds a call frame, and boxing (std::function, dynamic dispatch, interface wrappers) can make composition measurably slower than a hand-fused loop in tight loops.
Wrap the chain in a Trace or tap helper during development to observe intermediate values without breaking the point-free style; remove or disable in production.

When a step can fail or return nothing, lift the chain into a Result/Option/monad layer and use its andThen/flatMap/bind combinator instead of raw composition — raw compose silently passes error values to the next step.
